chapter_sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Reproductive processes give rise to new individuals that are similar to their parents, but subtly different.
Some amount of VARIATION is produced even during asexual reproduction; sexual reproduction maximises the number of successful variations.

In a field of sugarcane (asexual reproduction) there is very little variation among individual plants, but in animals including human beings (sexual reproduction) quite distinct variations are visible.
This chapter studies the mechanism by which variations are CREATED and INHERITED.
The two main areas of study are: how variation accumulates during reproduction, and how traits are inherited (Mendel's rules and sex determination).

DEFINITION: ACCUMULATION OF VARIATION DURING REPRODUCTION is the process by which inherited differences and newly created differences build up in successive generations of organisms produced through reproduction.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Inheritance from the previous generation provides both a common basic body design AND subtle changes in it for the next generation.
The second generation will have differences that they inherit from the first generation, as well as newly created differences.
In ASEXUAL REPRODUCTION (e.g. a bacterium dividing), the resultant individuals are very similar, with only very minor differences caused by small inaccuracies in DNA copying.
In SEXUAL REPRODUCTION, even greater diversity is generated.
All variations in a species do NOT have equal chances of surviving in their environment. Depending on the nature of variations, different individuals have different kinds of advantages.
Example: Bacteria that can withstand heat will survive better in a heat wave.
SELECTION of variants by environmental factors forms the basis for EVOLUTIONARY PROCESSES.

sections.label: DIAGRAMS IN THIS TOPIC:
sections.raw: - Figure 8.1: Creation of diversity over succeeding generations (described under the chapter level above), illustrating how a single organism gives rise to individuals with both inherited and newly created differences.

sections.label: EXERCISE 8.1 (In-text QUESTIONS box, page 59):

items.question: If a trait A exists in 10% of a population of an asexually reproducing species and a trait B exists in 60% of the same population, which trait is likely to have arisen earlier?
items.answer: Trait B is likely to have arisen earlier. In an asexually reproducing species, variation accumulates slowly over many generations. A trait present in a larger fraction of the population (60%) has had more time to spread to descendants, so it must have appeared earlier than trait A, which is present in only 10% of the population and has had less time to spread.

items.question: How does the creation of variations in a species promote survival?
items.answer:
Variations give different individuals different kinds of advantages. When the environment changes (for example a heat wave), individuals carrying a useful variation (such as heat tolerance) survive better and reproduce. Thus variations allow at least some members of the species to survive changing conditions, ensuring the survival of the species as a whole and forming the basis of evolution.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

items.question: What is variation? Give one example.
items.answer: VARIATION is the difference seen among individuals of the same species, arising during the process of reproduction. Example: Among human beings (who reproduce sexually), distinct variations are visible such as differences in height, skin colour and earlobe type.

items.question: Why is there very little variation among sugarcane plants in a field but distinct variation among human beings?
items.answer: Sugarcane reproduces ASEXUALLY, so the offspring are nearly identical copies of the parent with only minor differences from DNA copying errors. Human beings reproduce SEXUALLY, which maximises the number of successful variations, producing distinct visible differences among individuals.

items.question: How does variation arise during asexual reproduction? Explain with an example.
items.answer: During asexual reproduction (for example, a bacterium dividing into two), the DNA is copied. Small INACCURACIES occur during DNA copying, producing very minor differences between the resulting individuals. For example, when one bacterium divides and then the resultant two bacteria divide again, the four bacteria are very similar but show very minor differences generated by these copying errors. These accumulate slowly over many generations.

items.question: Explain how selection of variants by the environment forms the basis of evolution.
items.answer: Different individuals of a species carry different variations, and these do not all have equal chances of survival. The environment "selects" those variants that have an advantage in the prevailing conditions. For example, bacteria that can withstand heat survive better during a heat wave, while others die. The surviving variants reproduce and pass on the advantageous trait. Over many generations, this SELECTION of useful variants by environmental factors changes the population, which forms the basis for evolutionary processes.

items.question: Compare the amount of variation produced in asexual reproduction and sexual reproduction, explaining the reason for the difference.
items.answer: In ASEXUAL reproduction, the offspring are produced from a single parent by DNA copying. Variation is small and arises only from minor inaccuracies during DNA copying, so individuals are very similar. In SEXUAL reproduction, genetic material comes from two parents and combines in new ways, so a much greater diversity of variations is generated. Therefore sexual reproduction produces far more variation than asexual reproduction, which increases the chances that some individuals survive a changing environment.

items.question: With reference to Figure 8.1, explain how diversity accumulates over succeeding generations and why this is important for a species.
items.answer:
Figure 8.1 shows an original organism at the top that gives rise to two individuals similar in body design but with subtle differences. Each of these in turn gives rise to two more individuals in the next generation. By the third generation, the four individuals in the bottom row are all different from each other. Some of these differences are unique (newly created), while others are inherited from their parents who were themselves different.
This shows that each generation provides both a common basic body design AND subtle changes. Over successive generations, inherited differences combine with newly created differences, so diversity keeps accumulating.
This accumulation is important because the variety of variations means that when the environment changes, at least some individuals are likely to have a trait suited to the new conditions. Those individuals survive and reproduce, so the species as a whole survives. Thus accumulation of variation ensures the long-term survival and evolution of the species.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

items.question: In which type of reproduction is the greatest diversity generated?
items.explanation: Sexual reproduction combines genetic material from two parents, generating greater diversity. The others are asexual and produce very similar offspring.

items.question: Minor differences between individuals produced by asexual reproduction are mainly due to:
items.explanation: In asexual reproduction, variation arises only from small errors during DNA copying. The other options do not apply to single-parent asexual reproduction.

items.question: Bacteria that can withstand heat survive better in a heat wave. This is an example of:

options.B: Selection of variants by the environment

items.explanation: The environment selects the heat-tolerant variant, which survives and reproduces. This selection by environmental factors is the basis of evolution.

items.question: A trait present in 60% of an asexually reproducing population, compared to a trait present in 10%, most likely:
items.explanation: A more widespread trait has had more time to spread through generations, so it arose earlier. The 10% trait is newer.

items.question: Selection of variants by environmental factors forms the basis for:
items.explanation: Environmental selection of advantageous variants over generations drives evolution. It is not limited to asexual reproduction and does not cause loss of all variation.

DEFINITION: HEREDITY is the reliable inheritance of traits and characteristics from parents to offspring. The rules of heredity determine the process by which the most obvious outcome of reproduction - the generation of individuals of similar design - is achieved while still allowing variation.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: The most obvious outcome of the reproductive process is the generation of individuals of similar design.
The rules of heredity determine how traits and characteristics are reliably inherited.
This topic looks closely at these rules through inherited traits, Mendel's experiments, how traits get expressed, and sex determination.

items.question: Define heredity.
items.answer: HEREDITY is the passing on of characters or traits from parents to their offspring through reproduction. The rules of heredity determine how traits and characteristics are reliably inherited from one generation to the next.

items.question: What is the most obvious outcome of the reproductive process?
items.answer: The most obvious outcome of the reproductive process is the GENERATION OF INDIVIDUALS OF SIMILAR DESIGN, i.e. offspring that resemble their parents, with traits reliably inherited according to the rules of heredity.

items.question: Why does each trait in a child have two versions?
items.answer: Both the father and the mother contribute practically EQUAL amounts of genetic material (DNA) to the child. This means that for each trait there is one version influenced by the paternal DNA and one influenced by the maternal DNA. Therefore for each trait there are TWO versions in each child, one inherited from each parent.

items.question: A child bears the basic features of a human being but does not look exactly like its parents. Explain why.
items.answer: A child inherits all the basic FEATURES of a human being because it receives a common basic body design through genetic material from both parents. However, it does not look exactly like either parent because (i) it receives a mixture of genetic material from two parents, combining their traits in new ways, and (ii) human populations show a great deal of variation. The combination of inherited traits from both parents along with this variation makes each individual unique.

items.question: How do both parents contribute to the traits of a child? Why is each germ cell important here?
items.answer: Both the father and the mother contribute practically equal amounts of genetic material (DNA) to the child, so for each trait there are two versions in the child - one from each parent. For this mechanism to work, each pea plant or organism must have two sets of all genes (one inherited from each parent), and each GERM CELL (gamete) must have only ONE gene set. When two germ cells combine, the two single sets join to restore the full set of two, ensuring equal contribution from both parents.

items.question: List the four areas studied under heredity (8.2) in this chapter and briefly state what each deals with.
items.answer:
The four sub-topics studied under Heredity are:
(1) INHERITED TRAITS (8.2.1) - deals with the similarities and differences between a child and its parents; a child bears all basic features of a human being but shows variation.
(2) RULES FOR THE INHERITANCE OF TRAITS - MENDEL'S CONTRIBUTIONS (8.2.2) - deals with Mendel's pea-plant experiments showing dominant and recessive traits and independent inheritance.
(3) HOW DO THESE TRAITS GET EXPRESSED? (8.2.3) - deals with how DNA makes proteins (enzymes/hormones) so that genes control characteristics or traits.
(4) SEX DETERMINATION (8.2.4) - deals with how the sex of an individual is decided, in human beings by the sex chromosomes X and Y.
Together these explain how variations are created and reliably inherited.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

items.question: The reliable passing on of traits from parents to offspring is called:
items.explanation: Heredity is the inheritance of traits from parents to offspring. The other terms describe related but different concepts.

items.question: For each trait, how many versions does a child have?
items.explanation: Each parent contributes one version of genetic material, so there are two versions of each trait in the child.

items.question: Both father and mother contribute to a child:

options.B: Practically equal amounts of genetic material

items.explanation: Both paternal and maternal DNA contribute practically equally, giving two versions of each trait.

items.question: For the mechanism of inheritance to work, each germ cell must carry:
items.explanation: Each germ cell carries one gene set; when two germ cells combine, the full set of two is restored.

items.question: A child resembles a human being in basic features but differs from its parents mainly because:

options.B: It receives a mixture of genes from two parents plus population variation

items.explanation: The mixture of genetic material from both parents combined with natural variation makes each individual unique while keeping basic human features.

Human populations show a great deal of VARIATION.
Free earlobes and attached earlobes are two variant traits found in human populations (Fig. 8.2).
The lowest part of the ear, called the EARLOBE, is closely attached to the side of the head in some people (attached) and free in others (free).
The pattern of such traits among students and their parents can be studied to suggest a rule for inheritance.

items.question: What are free and attached earlobes? Why are they studied?
items.answer: The lowest part of the ear is the EARLOBE. In some people the earlobe is free (hanging), while in others it is closely ATTACHED to the side of the head. They are two variant traits found in human populations and are studied as examples of INHERITED TRAITS passed from parents to offspring.

items.question: Why does a child resemble its parents in basic features yet not look exactly like them?
items.answer: A child inherits all the basic FEATURES of a human being because it receives genetic material giving a common body design. However, it does not look exactly like its parents because it receives a mixture of traits from both parents and because human populations show a great deal of VARIATION. This combination makes each child similar in basic design but unique in appearance.

items.question: Describe how Activity 8.1 helps in understanding the inheritance of traits.

In Activity 8.1, the ears of all students in a class are observed, and a list is made of those with free and attached earlobes, calculating the percentage of each type. The earlobes of each student's parents are then found out and correlated with the student's own earlobe type. By comparing the earlobe types of students with those of their parents, a relationship is seen, and a possible RULE for inheritance of earlobe type can be suggested. This shows that such traits are inherited from parents to offspring.

subtopics.subtopic_name: RULES FOR THE INHERITANCE OF TRAITS - MENDEL'S CONTRIBUTIONS

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Both father and mother contribute practically EQUAL amounts of genetic material to the child, so for each trait there are two versions in each child.

GREGOR JOHANN MENDEL (1822-1884) was educated in a monastery, studied science and mathematics at the University of Vienna, and grew peas in his monastery. He was the first to keep COUNT of individuals showing a particular trait in each generation, which helped him arrive at the laws of inheritance.
Mendel used contrasting visible characters of garden peas: round/wrinkled seeds, tall/short plants, white/violet flowers, and so on.
He crossed a tall plant with a short plant and calculated the percentages of tall or short progeny.
F1 GENERATION (first progeny): all plants were TALL; there were no medium-height (halfway) plants. So only ONE parental trait was seen, not a mixture.
When F1 tall plants were self-pollinated, the F2 GENERATION progeny were not all tall: about ONE QUARTER (1/4) of them were short.
This shows both tallness and shortness traits were inherited in the F1 plants, but only the tallness trait was expressed.
Mendel proposed that two copies of factor (now called GENES) controlling a trait are present in a sexually reproducing organism; these two may be identical or different depending on parentage.
A single copy of 'T' (TT or Tt) makes the plant tall; both copies must be 't' (tt) for the plant to be short.
Traits that behave like 'T' are DOMINANT traits; traits that behave like 't' are RECESSIVE traits.
When two traits are studied together (e.g. seed shape and seed colour), they are inherited INDEPENDENTLY: in F2, new combinations appear (tall with wrinkled seeds, short with round seeds, etc.).
For a dihybrid cross (e.g. round-yellow x wrinkled-green), the F2 phenotype ratio is 9:3:3:1 (round-yellow : round-green : wrinkled-yellow : wrinkled-green).

sections.label: DIAGRAMS IN THIS TOPIC:
sections.raw:
- Figure 8.3: Inheritance of traits over two generations. A cross of Tall (TT) x Short (tt) gives an F1 of all Tall offspring (Tt). When F1 (Tt) x F1 (Tt) is self-crossed, the F2 generation shows Tall (TT), Tall (Tt), Tall (Tt) and Short (tt) - i.e. a 1:2:1 ratio of TT : Tt : tt and a 3:1 ratio of tall : short.
- Figure 8.4: P generation cross fertilisation followed by F1 self fertilisation giving an F2 with a 3:1 ratio.
- Figure 8.5: Independent inheritance of two separate traits, shape and colour of seeds. A cross of RR yy (round, green) x rr YY (wrinkled, yellow) gives F1 Rr Yy (round, yellow). Self-crossing F1 Rr Yy x Rr Yy produces an F2 with the gametes RY, Ry, rY, ry combining in a Punnett square (RRYY, RRYy, RrYY, RrYy, RRYy, RRyy, RrYy, Rryy, RrYY, RrYy, rrYY, rrYy, RrYy, Rryy, rrYy, rryy). The F2 results are 315 round-yellow (9), 108 round-green (3), 101 wrinkled-yellow (3) and 32 wrinkled-green (1) out of 556 seeds, giving the 9:3:3:1 ratio.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 8.2:
sections.aim: To design an experiment confirming the F2 trait ratio in Mendel's monohybrid cross (Fig. 8.3).
sections.materials: Reference to Figure 8.3 (the tall/short pea-plant cross and its F2 generation).
procedure: In Fig. 8.3, work out what experiment would be done to confirm that the F2 generation did in fact have a 1:2:1 ratio of TT, Tt and tt trait combinations.
sections.observation: The F2 plants appear in a 3:1 ratio of tall to short, but TT and Tt plants both look tall and cannot be told apart by appearance.
sections.conclusion:
To confirm the 1:2:1 (TT:Tt:tt) ratio, each F2 tall plant must be self-pollinated (or test-crossed). Pure tall (TT) plants give only tall offspring, while Tt plants give both tall and short offspring in a 3:1 ratio. This separates the TT plants from the Tt plants and confirms the underlying 1:2:1 genotype ratio.

items.question: Who was Gregor Johann Mendel and why is he important in the study of heredity?
items.answer: GREGOR JOHANN MENDEL (1822-1884) was a monk educated in a monastery who studied science and mathematics and grew peas. He was the FIRST to keep count of individuals showing a particular trait in each generation, which helped him arrive at the LAWS OF INHERITANCE.

items.question: What are dominant and recessive traits?
items.answer: A DOMINANT trait is one that is expressed even when only one copy of its factor is present (behaves like 'T'). A RECESSIVE trait is one that is expressed only when both copies of its factor are present (behaves like 't'); it is masked when a dominant copy is present.

items.question: Describe the F1 and F2 results when Mendel crossed tall and short pea plants.
items.answer: When Mendel crossed a tall plant (TT) with a short plant (tt), all the F1 progeny were TALL (Tt) - there were no medium-height plants, so only one parental trait appeared. When these F1 tall plants were self-pollinated, the F2 progeny were not all tall: about one quarter were SHORT. This gave a 3:1 ratio of tall to short, showing both traits were inherited but only tallness was expressed in F1.

items.question: Explain, using TT, Tt and tt, why F1 plants are all tall but F2 plants include short plants.
items.answer: A tall parent is TT and a short parent is tt. In the F1 cross, each offspring gets one 'T' from the tall parent and one 't' from the short parent, so all F1 plants are Tt. Since a single 'T' is enough to make a plant tall (T is dominant), all F1 plants are tall. When Tt plants are self-pollinated, the F2 plants can be TT, Tt or tt in a 1:2:1 ratio. TT and Tt plants are tall (three quarters), but tt plants are SHORT (one quarter) because both copies are recessive 't'. This is why short plants reappear in F2.

items.question: What did Mendel observe about the inheritance of two traits together, and what does it tell us? Use seed shape and seed colour as an example.
items.answer: When Mendel bred a tall plant with round seeds together with a short plant with wrinkled seeds, the F1 were all tall with round seeds (so tallness and round seeds are dominant). On self-pollinating the F1, the F2 included not only the parental combinations but also NEW combinations - tall plants with wrinkled seeds and short plants with round seeds. For seed shape and seed colour (round-yellow x wrinkled-green), the F2 appears in a 9:3:3:1 ratio. This tells us that the two traits are inherited INDEPENDENTLY of each other.

items.question: Describe Mendel's contributions to the rules of inheritance, including dominant/recessive traits and independent inheritance.
items.answer:
Gregor Johann Mendel used contrasting visible characters of garden peas (round/wrinkled seeds, tall/short plants, white/violet flowers, etc.) and was the first to keep count of individuals showing each trait in every generation.
(1) DOMINANCE: On crossing tall (TT) and short (tt) plants, all F1 were tall (Tt); on self-pollination, F2 showed tall and short in a 3:1 ratio. He concluded that two copies of a factor (gene) control a trait. A single 'T' makes a plant tall, so 'T' is DOMINANT; both copies must be 't' for a short plant, so 't' is RECESSIVE.
(2) TWO FACTORS PER TRAIT: He proposed that two copies of the gene for each trait are present, which may be identical (TT, tt) or different (Tt) depending on parentage.
(3) INDEPENDENT INHERITANCE: When two traits (e.g. seed shape and seed colour) are followed together, new combinations appear in F2 (round-yellow, round-green, wrinkled-yellow, wrinkled-green in a 9:3:3:1 ratio). This shows that different traits are inherited INDEPENDENTLY.
These observations form the basic rules of inheritance still used today.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

items.explanation: Mendel used contrasting visible characters of garden peas. The other organisms were not used by Mendel.

items.explanation: T is dominant, so all F1 (Tt) plants are tall; there are no medium-height plants.

items.explanation: F2 of a monohybrid cross gives a 3:1 phenotype ratio (tall:short). 1:2:1 is the genotype ratio.

items.explanation: Self-crossing Tt x Tt gives genotypes in a 1:2:1 ratio of TT:Tt:tt. 3:1 is the phenotype ratio.

items.explanation: New combinations appearing in F2 show the two traits are inherited independently of each other.

items.explanation: A dihybrid cross gives a 9:3:3:1 ratio (315:108:101:32 seeds), confirming independent inheritance.

subtopics.subtopic_name: HOW DO THESE TRAITS GET EXPRESSED?

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Cellular DNA is the information source for making PROTEINS in the cell.
A section of DNA that provides information for one protein is called a GENE.
Proteins control characteristics. Example: plants have HORMONES that can trigger growth, so plant height depends on the amount of a particular plant hormone.
The amount of plant hormone made depends on the EFFICIENCY of the process for making it, which depends on an ENZYME.
If the enzyme works efficiently, a lot of hormone is made and the plant is TALL.
If the gene for that enzyme has an ALTERATION that makes the enzyme less efficient, less hormone is made and the plant is SHORT.
Thus GENES CONTROL CHARACTERISTICS, or traits.
Both parents must contribute equally to the DNA of the progeny; both must contribute a copy of the same gene, so each organism has TWO sets of all genes - one inherited from each parent.
For this mechanism to work, each GERM CELL must have only ONE gene set, so that when two germ cells combine the full two sets are restored.

items.question: What is a gene?
items.answer: A GENE is a section of DNA that provides the information for making one PROTEIN in the cell. Genes control the characteristics or traits of an organism by directing protein synthesis.

items.question: How does a gene control the height of a plant? Explain with the role of an enzyme.
items.answer: Plant height depends on the amount of a plant HORMONE that triggers growth. The amount of hormone made depends on the efficiency of an ENZYME, which is made according to information in a gene. If the gene makes an efficient enzyme, a lot of hormone is produced and the plant is TALL. If the gene is altered so the enzyme is less efficient, less hormone is made and the plant is SHORT. Thus the gene controls the trait of height.

items.question: Explain why each organism has two sets of genes and why each germ cell must have only one set.
items.answer:
Both parents contribute practically equal amounts of DNA to the progeny, and both contribute a copy of the SAME gene for each trait. This means each organism (such as a pea plant) must have TWO sets of all genes, one inherited from each parent. For this to work without doubling the gene number each generation, each GERM CELL (gamete) must carry only ONE set of genes. When two germ cells (one from each parent) combine during fertilisation, the two single sets join to restore the full TWO sets, keeping the number of genes constant and ensuring equal contribution from both parents.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

items.question: A section of DNA that provides information for one protein is called a:
items.explanation: A gene is the DNA section coding for one protein. The others are not definitions of a gene.

items.question: Genes control the traits of an organism by controlling the making of:
items.explanation: DNA (genes) carries information to make proteins, which control characteristics.

items.question: A plant is tall because the enzyme made by its gene is efficient and produces:
items.explanation: An efficient enzyme makes a lot of growth hormone, so the plant grows tall.

items.question: If a gene is altered so its enzyme is less efficient, the plant will most likely be:
items.explanation: A less efficient enzyme makes less hormone, so the plant is short.

items.question: Each germ cell carries only one set of genes so that when two germ cells combine:

options.A: The gene number doubles every generation
options.B: The full two sets of genes are restored

items.explanation: Two single sets join at fertilisation to restore two sets, keeping gene number constant across generations.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Different species use very different strategies for sex determination.
Some species rely entirely on ENVIRONMENTAL cues; for example, in some reptiles the temperature at which fertilised eggs are kept determines whether the animals will be male or female.
In other animals, such as snails, individuals can CHANGE sex, showing that sex is not always genetically determined.
In HUMAN BEINGS, the sex of an individual is largely GENETICALLY determined - the genes inherited from parents decide whether we will be boys or girls.
Not all human chromosomes are paired in the same way: humans have 22 pairs that are perfectly matched, plus one pair of SEX CHROMOSOMES.
WOMEN have a perfect pair of sex chromosomes, both called X (XX).
MEN have a mismatched pair: one normal-sized X and one short chromosome called Y (XY).
All children inherit an X chromosome from their MOTHER, regardless of whether they are boys or girls.

The sex of a child is determined by what is inherited from the FATHER: a child who inherits an X chromosome from the father is a GIRL (XX); a child who inherits a Y chromosome from the father is a BOY (XY).
Half the children will be boys and half will be girls.

- Figure 8.6: Sex determination in human beings. A male (XY) and a female (XX) produce gametes; the female produces only X gametes while the male produces X and Y gametes. When an X gamete from the father combines with the mother's X, the zygote is XX and the offspring is a female; when a Y gamete from the father combines with the mother's X, the zygote is XY and the offspring is a male.

items.question: How many pairs of chromosomes do human beings have, and what is special about one pair?
items.answer: Human beings have 23 pairs of chromosomes. Of these, 22 pairs are perfectly matched, while ONE pair - the SEX CHROMOSOMES - is special: it is XX in women (a perfect pair) and XY in men (a mismatched pair with one short Y chromosome).

items.question: What are the sex chromosomes of a human male and a human female?
items.answer: A human FEMALE has two X chromosomes (XX), a perfect pair. A human MALE has one X chromosome and one Y chromosome (XY), a mismatched pair.

items.question: Give two examples of sex determination methods that are different from those in human beings.
items.answer: (1) In some REPTILES, sex is determined by the ENVIRONMENT - the temperature at which the fertilised eggs are kept decides whether the offspring will be male or female. (2) In SNAILS, individuals can CHANGE their sex, so sex is not genetically fixed. These differ from human beings, where sex is largely genetically determined by the X and Y chromosomes.

items.question: Explain how the sex of a child is determined in human beings.
items.answer: In humans, the mother is XX and the father is XY. All eggs (gametes) from the mother carry an X chromosome. The father's sperm may carry either an X or a Y chromosome. If a sperm carrying X fertilises the egg, the child is XX (a GIRL); if a sperm carrying Y fertilises the egg, the child is XY (a BOY). Therefore all children inherit an X from the mother, and the sex of the child is decided by whether they inherit an X or a Y from the FATHER. About half the children are boys and half are girls.

items.question: Why is it the father, and not the mother, who determines the sex of the child?
items.answer: The mother (XX) can only give an X chromosome to every child, so she always contributes X regardless of the child's sex. The father (XY) can give either an X or a Y chromosome. If he contributes X, the child is XX (girl); if he contributes Y, the child is XY (boy). Since the child's sex depends on whether the father's gamete carries X or Y, it is the FATHER (the paternal chromosome) that determines the sex of the child.

items.question: Describe sex determination in human beings with reference to Figure 8.6, and compare it with sex determination in some other species.
items.answer:
In human beings (Fig. 8.6), the female has the sex chromosomes XX and the male has XY. The female produces gametes that all carry an X chromosome, while the male produces two kinds of gametes - half carrying X and half carrying Y. At fertilisation, the mother always supplies an X. If the father's gamete carries X, the zygote is XX and develops into a GIRL; if the father's gamete carries Y, the zygote is XY and develops into a BOY. Thus the sex of the child depends on the paternal chromosome, and roughly half the children are boys and half are girls.
This is GENETIC sex determination. In other species it can be different: in some reptiles, sex is decided by the ENVIRONMENT (the temperature at which eggs are kept), and in snails, individuals can even CHANGE their sex. So while human sex is largely genetically determined by X and Y chromosomes, many other organisms determine sex by environmental or other means.

items.question: The sex chromosomes of a human female are:
items.explanation: Human females have two X chromosomes (XX). XY is male.

items.question: The sex chromosomes of a human male are:
items.explanation: Human males have one X and one Y chromosome (XY).

items.question: All children inherit which chromosome from their mother?
items.explanation: The mother is XX and can only contribute an X chromosome to every child.

items.question: The sex of a human child is determined by the chromosome inherited from the:
items.explanation: The father contributes either X (girl) or Y (boy); the mother always gives X, so the father decides the sex.

items.question: In some reptiles, the sex of the offspring is determined by:

options.A: The X and Y chromosomes only
options.B: The temperature at which the eggs are kept

items.explanation: In some reptiles, environmental temperature during incubation determines sex, unlike in humans.

items.question: A child who inherits a Y chromosome from the father will be a:
items.explanation: An X from mother plus a Y from father gives XY, which is a boy. An X from the father would give a girl.
